Furthermore, because the death-and-rebirth of the fragmented existence (pariccheda-maraṇa) has been exhausted while the death-and-rebirth of transformation (pariṇāma-maraṇa) has not yet been eliminated, the interval between these two deaths is distinguished as "with remainder" (sopadhiśeṣa) and "without remainder" (nirupadhiśeṣa); thus it is said that [this state] is the Middle Way, and so forth.
"‘If sentient beings abide in the second stage’ and below, this combines with the third [stage] as they approach the place of treasure.
The preceding section had two parts; now, this combination also has two:
‘If sentient beings abide in the second stage’—this combines with the knowledge of having already found rest."
"Then the Tathāgata immediately preached for them," and so forth, refers to leading [the disciples] toward the place of treasure. "Just as that guide...

and so forth, is the second section: restating the analogy and applying it to the teaching. It restates the analogy of retreating to apply it to the bestowal of the three vehicles, and restates the analogy of the extinction of transformation to apply it to the manifestation of the One Vehicle, as explained in detail in the text.
Second, the verse section consists of forty-nine and a half verses.
Of these, the first twenty-two and a half verses praise the causes for establishing a karmic connection;
the subsequent twenty-seven verses praise the second part, the actual establishment of the karmic connection.
Regarding the causes, there are those that are distant and those that are proximate. Now, the first twelve lines of verse praise the distant cause;
the subsequent ten and a half lines, beginning with "The World-Honored One of Immeasurable Wisdom," praise the proximate cause.

Regarding the preceding section on the distant past, there are two parts. First, six lines of verse describe the Great Attainment of Enlightenment; second, six lines of verse describe the Brahmās of the ten directions coming to request the turning of the Wheel of Dharma.

Within the first part concerning the attainment of enlightenment, there are five sections. Now, the first three lines of verse describe the events prior to the second stage, when he was about to attain enlightenment;
next, from "After ten minor kalpas had passed" onwards, the second section consists of one line of verse, describing the third stage, the actual attainment of enlightenment.

Next, from "The sixteen sons of that Buddha" onwards is the third section, consisting of two lines. This verse praises the request for the turning of the wheel of Dharma made by the fifty-sixth son, while simultaneously praising the fourth event—the offering of worship by the retinue after his attainment of enlightenment; it briefly omits a verse on the first event, the long duration of the Buddha's lifespan.
The six lines beginning with "The World-Honored One is extremely difficult to encounter" eulogize the invitation by the Brahmās of the ten directions.
Of these, the first line above eulogizes the majestic radiance that shook and shone;
the second section, consisting of five lines beginning with "The Brahmās of the East," eulogizes the Brahmās of the ten directions seeking out the light and coming forth.
Among these, the first three stanzas pertain to the eastern direction; the following two stanzas summarize the nine directions as a whole.
From "The World-Honored One of Immeasurable Wisdom" onwards, the second section consists of ten and a half stanzas, which praise the proximate causes (*upaniṣad*).
Of the two [sections] above, the first five lines now constitute the verse on the first turning of the wheel of Dharma for the two vehicles;

the subsequent second section, from "At that time, the sixteen princes" onwards, consists of five and a half lines and constitutes the verse on the second request to turn the wheel of the Mahāyāna Dharma.
The first section above is further divided into three parts. First, from "Immeasurable" (*apramāṇa*) downward, for half a line, this verse praises the first [act]: accepting the invitation.
Second, from "For their sake he proclaims" (*deśayituṃ*) downward, for one and a half lines, this verse praises the second [act]: correctly turning the wheel of the Two Vehicles (*dharma-cakra*).
Third, from "Proclaiming clearly" (*viśadīkṛtya*) downward, for three lines, this verse praises the third [act]: the assembly hearing the Dharma and attaining the Way.
"Then the sixteen princes," from here down for five lines and a half, is the second section: the princes' renewed request.
This contains seven parts;
the first two lines are a verse summarizing the renunciation of the first prince.
Next, from "All together requested him" onwards, the second section consists of one and a half lines, which versifies the second point: the formal request to turn the Mahāyāna wheel;
next, from "The Buddha knew the youth" onwards, the third section consists of two lines, which versifies the preaching of the Vaipulya *Prajñāpāramitā* during the interval of twenty thousand kalpas;

next, from "When he preached this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*" onwards, the fourth section consists of half a line, which formally versifies the fourth point: the acceptance of the request to preach the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*.

Next, from "After that Buddha had finished preaching the sutra" onwards is the fifth section, consisting of one line, which praises the seventh point: that after preaching the sutra, he entered meditative absorption; it briefly omits the praise for the third point (the eighty thousand people led by the father king who sought to leave home), the fifth point (that among the assembly who heard the sutra, some understood while others did not), and the sixth point (the long duration of time during which the sutra was preached).
From "These śrāmaṇeras... below, there are twenty-seven lines that verse the formal conclusion of the connection (*saṃbandha*).

The preceding prose consists of two parts; here, first, eight lines verse the teaching by way of Dharma (*dharmadeśanā*), and next, nineteen lines verse the teaching by way of parable (*aupamyadeśanā*).

The discourse on the supreme Dharma consists of three parts. Now, the first three lines of verse constitute the first section: the past causal conditions; the next single line of verse constitutes the second section: their mutual encounter in the interim; and the subsequent four lines of verse constitute the third section: returning today to preach the Lotus Sutra.
In the past, there were four occasions for the establishment of karmic causes and conditions. First, the first one and a half lines of verse describe the Buddha entering meditative concentration.
Second, from "For immeasurable billions" onwards, the next one and a half lines describe the formal recitation and exposition.

Third, from "Each and every śrāmaṇera" onwards, the final line describes the benefits gained from hearing the Dharma; the fourth part—the Buddha’s emergence from concentration and his expression of praise—is omitted from the verse.
Next, from "After that Buddha’s parinirvāṇa" onwards, the second section consists of three lines, which versify their meeting in the interim.
From "These sixteen śrāmaṇeras" onwards, the third section consists of four lines, which versify the preaching of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* today.
The preceding section has two parts:
first, the correlation of the ancient and the modern, which includes both the present and the future; here, the first three lines of verse correlate the present master and disciples.

"By this fundamental cause and condition," and so forth, constitutes the second section, a single line of verse that returns to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*. Of the three parts in the preceding prose, the first phrase here corresponds to the first [part]: the purity of the assembly at that time; "by this fundamental cause and condition" indicates that the present assembly has now escaped calamity and their spiritual capacity has been awakened.

Next, from "now preaching the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*" onwards, the second section consists of three phrases, corresponding to the second [part]: the preaching of this sutra for their sake. The third part—the explanation of the meaning of opening up the three [vehicles]—is omitted from the verse.

Below the section on "the perilous and evil path," the second part consists of nineteen lines. These verses illustrate the analogy through its expansion and contraction: the first eleven and a half lines expand the analogy, while the final seven and a half lines contract it.

The preceding section provided two analogies; now, the first three lines of verse present the analogy of the five hundred *yojanas*, and the subsequent eight and a half lines of verse present the analogy of the guide.
Regarding the preceding five points concerning the "five hundred," here the first line of verse corresponds to the second point, the perilous and evil road;
next, from the words "countless tens of millions" (*asaṃkhyeya-koṭi*) onwards, the second half-line corresponds to the third point, the great multitude of people.
Next, from "That path is most... onwards is the third section, consisting of half a line, which versifies the first [point], the five hundred yojanas;
next, from "At that time there was a guide... onwards is the fourth section, consisting of one line, which versifies the fifth, the single guide;
and from "Possessing strong memory... onwards are three lines, which versify being wise and sagacious, but do not versify the fourth.
Following "All the people are weary," the second section consists of eight and a half lines, which versify the second analogy of the guide.
The preceding prose had three parts; now, this verse likewise versifies those three:
the first two characters versify the first part, the guide.

From "All were exhausted" onwards is the second section: five lines of three phrases each, in three-character units, which versifies the second analogy of the provisional establishment of the transformation city because the multitude grew weary and retreated;

next, from "The guide, having known this" onwards is the third section: two and a half lines, which versifies the third analogy of extinguishing the transformation [city] and leading them to the place of treasure.
The second section above contains two parts: first, the regression of indolence; second, the regression of reconnection.
Now, the first three lines of three characters each praise the regression of indolence, while the subsequent five lines praise the regression of reconnection through the performance of emanations.
Regarding the three types of regression and withdrawal mentioned above, the first—regression midway—is now omitted from the verse.

The preceding section connected regression with the composition of the transformative text; here, all are fully versified. The first line of the verse praises the second [point], the "sorrowful loss of the Great";
the subsequent two lines beginning with "seeking at that time" constitute the second part, praising the first [point], the "forming of a thought."
Next, from "He transforms it into a great city" onwards, the third section consists of two and a half lines, which versify the third [act]: the creation of the transformation.
This preceding text further divides into two parts; here, the first one and a half lines versify the actual illustration of creating the transformation.
"Various dwellings" refers to the objects of various contemplations on emptiness.
"Gardens and groves" refers to the groves of the untainted dharmas of the total retention (dhāraṇī) of the two vehicles.

The nine successive concentrations are the "canals," and the eight liberations are the "bathing pools. The "heavy gates" are the three gates of emptiness; furthermore, the heavy-emptiness samādhi and the knowledge of exhaustion and non-arising constitute the lofty towers and pavilions.
"Man and woman" refers to wisdom (*prajñā*) and meditative concentration (*samādhi*).

For one who understands through the contemplation of the mind: the essence of wisdom is all-encompassing like a city wall; wholesome dharmas are perfectly complete like the surrounding suburbs; ultimate emptiness serves as the dwelling. Rectitude and goodness can accomplish one's own practice, just as a man is capable of managing domestic affairs; while compassion transforms others externally, just as a woman goes out to attend to external matters.
Next, from "Having thus performed this transformation" onwards, the second section consists of one line, which versifies the aforementioned transformation.
Next, from "Once the people had entered" onwards, the fourth section consists of one line, which versifies the fourth [section], the entry into the city.

"Once the Guide knew they had rested," and so forth, is the third section, consisting of two and a half lines, which praises the third stage: the cessation of the transformation and the arrival at the place of treasure.
The preceding passage has two parts; here, first, one line praises the first part, "knowing they had rested";
next, from "assembling the multitude" onwards, the second part consists of two lines and one phrase, praising the cessation of the transformation and leading them toward the place of treasure.

"‘I am also likewise’ and below" constitutes the second section, consisting of seven and a half lines, which summarizes the second pair of similes. The first half-line summarizes the first of the two, the simile of the five hundred [servants], while the subsequent seven lines summarize the second, the simile of the guide.
The preceding section comprises five hundred verses, plus another four; now, only half of these are presented as a summary verse.
The two lines beginning with "Seeing those who seek the Way" summarize the analogy for indolence and retreat.

The preceding verse provides the analogy but does not provide the commentary on the middle path; now, one line combines the commentary on the exhaustion and retreat midway, and the following line provides the commentary on the combination of returning from that retreat to perform the work of transformation.

From "Since he already knows how to reach nirvana" onwards, the second section consists of five lines, which provide the commentary on the second point: the combined cessation and transformation leading to the place of treasure.
The preceding prose combined two sections; now the verse likewise has two parts:
the first half-verse praises the first [stage], "knowing the breath";

from "thereupon assembling the great assembly" onwards, the second part consists of three and a half verses, praising the second [stage], which combines cessation and transformation to lead [the beings] toward the place of treasure.
Within the verse on the transformation of the breath, there is the meaning of the secret treasury of the three virtues:

"You realize all-knowledge" is *prajñā* (wisdom); "possessing the thirty-two marks" is the *dharmakāya* (dharma-body); and "this is true cessation" is *vimukti* (liberation). That these three dharmas are neither vertical nor horizontal is precisely the vision of the Buddha-nature.
"The Guides of all Buddhas" and below—this single line serves as a summary verse.
Regarding the "Chapter on the Prediction for the Five Hundred Disciples": although this chapter records the predictions for twelve hundred [disciples], why is it titled "The Five Hundred"?
Five hundred [bodhisattvas] received their predictions with identical names, and five hundred verbally expressed their understanding; thus, this serves as the title for the chapter.
This chapter constitutes the second section within the discourse on causes and conditions (*nidāna*).
One must distinguish two types:
first, twelve hundred; second, two thousand. Regarding the twelve hundred, there are again two types:
First, the bestowal upon Pūrṇa; second, the bestowal upon the twelve hundred.
Regarding Pūrṇa, there are two parts:
first, his silent comprehension of the introduction; second, the Tathāgata’s formal prediction.
First, the joy of their attainment of understanding is described; second, their silent reflection and internal realization are described.
Regarding the joy, there are two parts:
first, the cause for their attainment of understanding; second, the joy of their attainment of understanding.
There are four reasons for attaining this understanding:
first, hearing the parables of the Dharma, wherein the three vehicles were opened up to reveal the One Vehicle;
second, the bestowing of predictions upon the five great disciples, such as Śāriputra; [and so forth].
Third, they further hear of the matters of karmic connections formed in past lives;
fourth, they further hear that the Buddhas and Tathāgatas possess the three types of unhindered penetration.

To perceive the distant past as if it were today is the power of great sovereign supernormal abilities, which sets them apart from the two vehicles and surpasses the limit of eighty thousand [kalpas].
If one "hears this wisdom from the Buddha," it refers to the revelation of the ultimate truth (*tattva*) within the chapters on "Expedient Means" (*upāya*) and "The Burning House";
"that which is taught according to what is appropriate through expedient means" refers to the disclosure of the provisional (*neyārtha*) in those two locations.
"The great disciples" refers to the opening of the provisional; "receiving the prediction of Bodhi" refers to the revelation of the ultimate;
"past-life causes and conditions" refers to the revelation of the ultimate; and "the power of supernatural transformations" refers to the opening of the provisional.

The passage beginning with "Attaining what was never before attained" describes his joy upon attaining understanding. First, it clarifies the internal joy of realization; next, it clarifies external expressions of reverence.

Because he had not heard this in the past—the revelation of the provisional to manifest the ultimate—and has now heard it, it says, "attaining what was never before attained. Because he has removed attachment to *nirvāṇa* and severed specific delusions, it says, "the mind is pure. Because the Buddha’s knowledge and vision have been opened, he is "leaping for joy. Since this attainment of understanding arises through the Buddha, he gives rise to reverence.
If we consider this in terms of the "original" and the "traced," it is merely a celebration of those who practice according to reality.
From the passage "and he had this thought" onwards, the text correctly elucidates the silent contemplation and realization.
First, it clarifies the silent contemplation and realization; next, it clarifies the silent seeking of the revelation of one's origin and the request for a prediction of enlightenment.
In the previous two cycles, those who attained awakening all spoke out to express their understanding; why is it that they now remain silent?
Previously, for the sake of those of inferior capacity who had not yet awakened, it was necessary to use explicit words to exhort and stir them;
now that those of inferior capacity have already awakened, there is nothing further to exhort or stir, and thus they remain silent and do not speak.

Furthermore, previously you merely accepted my explanation without seeking to reveal your true identity; in that case, there was no cause for suspicion. Now, however, you both understand and reveal yourself. Because you understand, you reflect; because you wish to avoid public censure, you remain silent. To reflect in silence is indeed most appropriate.

Furthermore, silent contemplation and understanding constitute the "great understanding," just as the silence of Vimalakīrti in the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa Sūtra* represents the true entry into the Dharma-gate of non-duality.

Moreover, the provisional and the ultimate are inconceivable; they are neither speech nor thought, yet they are expressed through speech and conceived through thought. Because they are expressed through that which is not speech, I have thus far articulated my understanding verbally; because they are conceived through that which is not thought, I now silently contemplate and understand them.
What was the intention behind not seeking to reveal his true identity previously?
It was because those of inferior capacity had not yet attained awakening; therefore, he did not seek to reveal his identity.
Now that those of inferior capacity have understood, his provisional manifestations are complete.
If one who possesses inferior faculties reveals their true status, it is known that those with middling or superior faculties likewise employ skillful means;
for if one were to rely solely on the superior or middling, it would be unsuitable for those of inferior capacity.
"The World-Honored One is most extraordinary, and his deeds are rare" refers to the realization of ultimate wisdom.
"To preach the Dharma in accordance with the various dispositions of worldly beings" refers to the mastery of provisional wisdom; it is the fundamental nature of the seven kinds of skillful means.
This summarizes the intent of the "Expedient Means" chapter (*Upāya-paṭala*) in revealing the ultimate truth while opening the provisional.

The phrase "to pull out sentient beings from their various attachments" summarizes the revelation of the ultimate truth while opening the provisional within the "Burning House" chapter (*Gṛha-dāha-paṭala*).

The phrase "We cannot fully proclaim the Buddha’s merits" refers to the preceding *Parable of the Medicinal Herbs*, which states that the Tathāgata possesses immeasurable merits beyond the reach of your abilities.
Since it is said that "words cannot proclaim it," it is also beyond the reach of thought.
The passage beginning with "Only the Buddha can know" refers to silently contemplating and seeking the revelation of his origins and requesting a prediction of his future enlightenment.
“We” refers to the traces left by all those who have universally invoked and requested [the Buddha’s awakening].
“Profound mind” (gambhīracitta) is the essence of the present, manifesting as these traces.

“Original vow” (pūrvapraṇidhāna) refers to the vow of great compassion: because one vows to transform others through great compassion, one makes a pledge; because one seeks to attain Buddhahood for oneself, one possesses a vow.
To request [the Buddha] to ascend is to seek the prediction of enlightenment (*vyākaraṇa*); to request him to descend and transform others is to seek the revelation of his origins.
Furthermore, because it proceeds from the profound mind, it clarifies how he has assisted the Buddha in proclaiming the transformation throughout the three periods of time;
because it proceeds from his original vow, he bestows the prediction upon him.
From "The Buddha told" onwards is the second section, in which the Buddha recounts and bestows a prediction (vyākaraṇa) upon him; this consists of both prose and verse.
The prose portion has two parts:
first, the recounting of his past and present manifestations (honji-suijaku), and second, the conferring of the prediction.
The first part has three sections:

first, the manifestation of the origin through practicing causes during the era of Śākyamuni; second, the revelation of the original nature through practicing causes during the eras of past Buddhas; third, the fulfillment of causal practices cultivated under the Buddhas of the three periods of time.
Regarding the revelation of the origins based on the causal practices of Śākyamuni Buddha, there are three further sections:

first, identifying the person; second, providing a general outline of the chapters on the fundamental and the manifested; and third, providing a detailed explanation of the fundamental and the manifested.
He immediately asks, "Do you see it? with two intentions:
first, whether they see its outward trace as small; second, whether they see its fundamental merit.
The multitude saw only that [Śāriputra] was a śrāvaka and could not know that he was originally a bodhisattva; therefore, it says, "they did not see him.
The passage beginning with "I have always praised him" serves to indicate his manifested status (traces).

In terms of his manifested traces (*vyañjana*), he is the foremost among those who preach the Dharma; yet, were it not for the wondrous essence of the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*), there would be no way to manifest these supreme traces.

Hitherto, it was only said that he was first among those who preach the Dharma within the realm of traces; now it is not so—he has long been foremost regarding the unsurpassed Dharma itself. This citation of the traces serves to reveal the essence.
The phrase "He also constantly praised" and what follows indicates his original ground (*mūlabhūmi*).
Because it encompasses the dharma-gates of myriad practices of merit and wisdom, it is called "various.
Since his original ground already possesses such various dharma-gates, how could his manifested traces (*nirmāṇakāya*) possibly be limited to those of the two vehicles?
This citation is presented to clarify the manifestation based on its source.
The section beginning with "Diligently protecting and upholding" is a detailed explanation.
"Aiding in the proclamation of my Dharma" refers specifically to aiding in the proclamation of the Dharma of the Half and Full Teachings within the stage of manifestation.
Manifesting as a śrāvaka of inferior capacity is the protection and assistance in proclaiming the *dadhi* (curd) Dharma;
manifesting in the Vaipulya sūtras while receiving censure and rebuke is the protection and assistance in proclaiming the *ghṛta* (fresh butter) Dharma;
and manifesting as the recipient of the *Prajñāpāramitā* is the protection and assistance in proclaiming the *pakvaghṛta* (matured butter) Dharma.
To attain awakening through the traces [of the teaching] in the *Lotus Sūtra* is precisely to protect, uphold, and assist in proclaiming the *Tetra-amṛta* (Butter-of-Butter) Dharma.
This is the meaning of what was stated above in the general introduction: "I constantly praise various merits."

Fully endowed with the merits of both the provisional and the real, he manifested his traces through the five flavors to assist the Buddha in maturing sentient beings of the true practice; is this not precisely the intent of diligent assistance in proclaiming the Dharma?
To separately explain the merits of the fundamental and the trace: "Able to instruct and guide the fourfold assembly" refers to the analytical teaching of the *half-syllable* (*ardhamātra*);
"fully explaining" refers to assisting in the proclamation of the *full-syllable* (*pūrṇamātra*) Prajñā teachings;
and "greatly benefiting" refers to assisting the Buddha in benefiting sentient beings through both the half- and full-syllable teachings.
"Companions in the holy life" refers to the disciples of both the provisional and ultimate vehicles who were transformed by his traces.
From "Having himself relinquished the Tathāgata" onwards, the merits of his original ground are described separately.
"Since his renunciation" refers to the period from when he attained wondrous enlightenment onwards.
"None can know" refers to the seven kinds of skillful means.

From the passage "You should not say that you merely assist in proclaiming my Dharma" onwards is the second section, which reveals his original practice during the eras of past Buddhas; it shows that he did not merely assist in proclaiming the *half* and *full* teachings under me, but likewise assisted in proclaiming the *half* and *full* teachings under Buddhas of long ago.

Taking what occurs today as the assistance in proclaiming [the teaching] serves to reveal the manifestation; taking what occurred in the past as the assistance in proclaiming [the teaching] serves to manifest the origin.
There are two ways of manifesting the origin:
first, the distant origin; second, the proximate origin.

The distant origins are profoundly remote and obscure, making them difficult to believe; therefore, I have omitted them from this account. I shall instead cite the ninety billion near origins, for one who possesses the wisdom of recollecting past lives can know these near origins. Thus, by citing the near, I provide proof for the distant.
In these nine billion verses, it fully elucidates how to assist the Buddha in proclaiming the teachings of the five flavors to bring sentient beings to maturity.
"Protecting and assisting in the proclamation" refers to assisting in the proclamation of the *ardhākṣara* (half-syllable) teaching, which is like the flavor of curd;
"the True Dharma of the Buddha" refers to assisting in the proclamation of the *vaipulya* teaching, which is like the flavor of clarified butter (*ghṛta*).

Furthermore, regarding those who "clearly understand the Dharma of Emptiness," this refers to assisting in the proclamation of the *Ghr̥tamaṇḍa-rasa* (Butter-cream) Dharma; it is also like the present Buddha turning the teaching to expound the *Prajñāpāramitā*, clarifying how the six *pāramitās* mutually encompass and revolve without obstruction. At the assemblies of ninety billion Buddhas, he likewise assisted in its proclamation no differently than now; yet the people of those Buddhas' worlds all regarded him as truly being a *śrāvaka*. At that time, since he had not yet revealed his true identity, they merely said he was commissioned to turn the *Prajñāpāramitā*, and did not say he was a Great Bodhisattva.

Regarding the phrase "transforming immeasurable sentient beings and causing them to establish themselves in *samyak-saṃbodhi*," this refers to assisting in the proclamation of the *Maṇḍa-rasa* (Cream-of-Curd) Dharma, which can be understood from the text as explained at length.
"Also under the seven Buddhas," and so forth, is the third section, which concerns the causes cultivated by the Buddhas of the three periods of time, as per the text.
This also follows the previous examples of assisting in the proclamation of the five flavors of the Half and Full Teachings, thereby benefiting those of both the Great and Small Vehicles.
